newsitem.title: UK: Airline safety shows big first half improvement.
newsitem.headline: Airline safety shows big first half improvement.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
World airline fatalities dropped sharply in the first half of this year, statistics published on Tuesday showed, and experts hope this trend will continue.
The safety record was almost too good to be true in the first six months of 1997, with only one major jet loss which killed 33 passengers, according to aviation information consultancy Airclaims.
This crash, of a China Southern Airlines Boeing 737-300 while landing in a thunderstorm at Shenzhen on May 8, also killed two crew members.
This compares with 401 deaths from four major jet crashes in the first half of 1996.
Last year as a whole was deadly for air travellers with 1,187 passenger deaths, the worst year in civil aviation history and three times worse than the previous year.

1996's chilling record includes the mid-air collision between a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Airlines Ilyushin IL-76 freighter near New Delhi which killed 349, and the still unsolved demise of TWA flight 800 which exploded while climbing over Long Island, New York, taking 230 lives.
Investigators have still not discovered the cause of the TWA Boeing 747 crash.

But experts point out that these spectacular disasters cloud the fact that plane crashes have remained fairly constant over the last 20 years while air travel has burgeoned from a pursuit of the rich to the mass market.
The increasing number of fatalities conceals the fact that statistically travel by air has become constantly safer.

Boeing, the world's leading maker of airliners, has said that this is not good enough. According to Boeing, if air travel continues to grow at the current rate without even more safety improvements, there would be a major accident somewhere in the world every week by the year 2005.

If the six month figures are regarded with some scepticism by regular travellers, wondering if potential disasters are merely waiting in a stack, they are undisputed good news for the insurance industry.
"The first half rate this year has been good, certainly as far as fatal accidents are concerned. Let's hope it continues and keep our fingers crossed," said Airclaims director Paul Hayes.
"If it does we will see a considerable drop for the year. But crashes come so randomly, we could have a bad spate, we've seen that in the past, it's very difficult to extrapolate," Hayes said.
Pointing to the tremendous long term improvement in safety, Hayes said that if the fatality rate was the same now as in the late 1940s, around 50,000 people would be killed each year.
"I don't think the industry could survive that," Hayes said.
Richard Whitaker, editor of Airline Business Magazine welcomed the figures, but warned about taking too much heart.

"You can't read too much into six months figures. The accident rate is very, very low, but one or two major accidents can distort the figure. It's best to look at an average of three to five years to even out the ups and downs," Whitaker said.
"Its undeniably great news for the insurance industry though," he said.
